description:
Welcome!

We are a team of three passionate engineering students from Alexandria University collaborating to create an impactful solution for the Martian Map challenge. Combining our backgrounds in software engineering, technology, and art, we aim to build creative solutions using open space and Earth observation data.
summary:
We developed ARES-NAV, an Astronaut Surface Navigation and Science HUD built for human Extravehicular Activities in Jezero Crater’s Western Delta.

While existing planetary viewers like JPL Mars Trek provide global orbital overviews, astronauts conducting surface Marswalks need hyperlocalized, real-time hazard routing. ARES-NAV fuses MRO HiRISE/CTX optical imagery, HiRISE digital elevation models for slope hazard detection, THEMIS thermal inertia, MGS TES spectral mineralogy, and USGS planetary geologic units  into an interactive tactical map powered by a React/TypeScript HUD and a Python/FastAPI pathfinding backend.

Astronauts can inspect visited rover waypoints with 360° Mastcam-Z surface panoramas, scout unvisited frontier terrain via sub-meter orbital zoom, and compute slope-constrained routes around steep escarpments and loose sand ripples.Additionally, crew members can flag newly discovered ground hazards as Shared Avoidance Zones, instantly syncing no-go polygons across all astronauts' maps and dynamically rerouting active paths to minimize risks and protect crew safety while maximizing astrobiological science return.
details:
ARES-NAV is a web-based mission-planning and real-time surface navigation system built for human Extravehicular in Jezero Crater’s Western Delta.

It works by merging 3 important features:

  1. Multi-Layer NASA Data Fusion: Inspired by NASA Worldview, astronauts can independently toggle and blend opacity across five distinct orbital and surface datasets:
    • Optical: High-resolution MRO HiRISE and CTX controlled mosaics for boulder-level obstacle spotting.
    • Topographic: HiRISE Digital Elevation Models processed into hypsometric elevation slices and slope-angle hazard heatmaps.
    • Thermal: Mars Odyssey THEMIS Night IR layers to distinguish solid basaltic bedrock from soft, high-sinkage dust and sand traps.
    • Spectral & Mineralogy: MGS TES spectral layers (high-calcium clinopyroxene, plagioclase feldspar, and surface dust cover) to highlight high-value sampling outcrops.
  2. Collaborative Dynamic Avoidance Zones: Because orbital imagery cannot catch every localized ground hazard (such as unstable rockslides, sharp regolith, or equipment hazards discovered mid-EVA), any astronaut can mark a dangerous location as an Avoidance Zone directly on the map. That hazard zone immediately syncs across the network for all other crew members, updating their shared HUD and forcing the dijkstra pathfinding engine to route all active and future Marswalks safely around the flagged perimeter.
  3. 360° Ground Recon vs. Unvisited Orbital Scouting: For visited rover stops along Perseverance’s traverse (such as Octavia E. Butler Landing), astronauts can inspect interactive 360° Mastcam-Z surface panoramas and live rover camera frames before departing. Clicking anywhere in unvisited frontier terrain triggers Orbital Recon Mode, smoothly zooming to maximum sub-meter orbital resolution and displaying coordinate telemetry so crews can safely scout unexplored targets.
  4. Slope-Constrained & Storm-Adaptive EVA Routing: Selecting a start and target waypoint computes an optimal walking path using a weighted dijkstra pathfinding engine. The router strictly enforces spacesuit slope limits (default ≤15°), skirts around loose eolian sand ripples in Séítah, and plots a real-time Elevation & Slope Profile.

These feature aims to deliver measurable benefits and intended impact by:

  • Real-Time Crew-to-Crew Protection: Eliminates repeated exposure to newly discovered surface dangers, if one astronaut encounters a hazard, every teammate's map and route updates automatically.
  • Suit Mobility & Space-Weather Safety: Prevents steep-slope falls and sand entrapment, and excess radiation exposure during sudden solar particle or dust events.
  • Higher Science Return per EVA: Bridges orbital mineral/geologic mapping with eye-level rover context so astronauts spend limited oxygen reserves sampling the highest-priority carbonate and clay outcrops.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Frontend (Astronaut HUD): React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React-Leaflet , Pannellum, Recharts, and Lucide Icons.
  • Backend (Geospatial & Pathfinding Engine): Python, FastAPI, Rasterio, NumPy, and SciPy for processing HiRISE GeoTIFF elevation rasters into slope-angle grids, hypsometric elevation masks and weighted dijkstra route.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered

  • Human-in-the-Loop Map Intelligence: Combines static orbital NASA datasets with live astronaut field observations via shared Avoidance Zones, bridging the gap between satellite resolution and boots-on-the-ground reality.
  • Dual-Mode Reconnaissance: Separates 360° Rover Ground Recon (at visited Perseverance stations) from Sub-Meter Orbital Recon (for unvisited frontier terrain).
  • Hypsometric Threshold Slicing: Lower elevation bands are masked out as transparent overlays so astronauts retain an unobstructed optical view of flat crater floors while steep delta scarps and crater rims stand out clearly.
